draft.title: Health across generations
card: A parent's health and circumstances can affect their children's health. These effects can continue to the next generation.
Some effects are biological. Parents can pass on genes that raise the risk of some conditions, and a mother's health in pregnancy can affect her baby.
Some effects come from circumstances. Income, housing, education and health habits shape the home a child grows up in.
A child raised with these advantages or disadvantages may then pass similar ones to their own children. This does not make poor health certain, since support and change can break the pattern.
draft.remember: Parents' health and circumstances can shape their children's health, and those children may pass it on.

a.q: Which example shows parents' circumstances affecting a child's health?
opts: A family on a low income can afford less nutritious food
A child is born with the same eye colour as a parent
A child breaks an arm while playing at school
A child catches a cold from a classmate
a.why: Income is a circumstance that shapes the food and housing a child has, so it can affect health. Eye colour is inherited but is not a health circumstance. A broken arm and a cold are not caused by parents' circumstances.
a.clue: Look for something about the home the child grows up in.

b.q: Tom's parents both had poor health habits, and Tom now has them. Which statement about Tom's own children is best?
opts: They may be affected, but support or change can reduce this
They will certainly have the same poor health as Tom
They will not be affected, as only parents' genes matter
They will be affected only if they live in the same house
b.why: Health effects can pass on, but they are not certain, and support or change can break the pattern. Saying they will certainly have poor health is too strong, and the effects are not only genetic.
b.clue: The card says the pattern can be broken.

a.best: A family on a low income can afford less nutritious food

b.best: They may be affected, but support or change can reduce this

problems.detail: The right option is the only hedged one ('may'). Every wrong option uses an absolute ('certainly', 'only'), so a test-wise student could pick it without knowing the idea.
